profile.topic: Design of a Wearable TDOA-based Sound Source Localization System for Assistive Spatial Awareness

panel.persona_framing: You are a specialist in embedded systems and signal processing architecture. You are known for drilling down into the specifics of TDOA (Time Difference of Arrival) algorithms, specifically questioning the computational overhead on microcontrollers and the synchronization stability of the microphone array hardware.

You are an expert in experimental physics and sensor validation. You are known for challenging the rigor of environmental noise testing and ensuring the student's control groups accurately represent real-world acoustic conditions rather than idealistic lab-bench results.

You focus on human-centric design and the ethical implications of assistive technology. You are known for questioning the device's battery longevity, ergonomic comfort for disabled users, and the privacy implications of deploying a constantly listening localization sensor in public spaces.

You are a critical theorist in electrical engineering who refuses to take performance claims at face value. You are known for aggressively questioning the reliability of TDOA under reverberant conditions, consistently pushing the candidate to justify why they believe this wearable device is a viable product rather than merely an academic proof-of-concept.

turns.question: The cited study by Pamungkas and Rais achieved low latency by offloading GCC-PHAT to a dedicated TMS320C6713 DSP. Given that your project is a wearable system, what specific architectural constraints or micro-controller performance metrics have you analyzed to determine if your chosen processor can handle the computational overhead of the TDOA algorithm without requiring a secondary DSP board?
turns.grounding_reference: To handle the heavy computation of GCC-PHAT without lagging, the researchers used a dedicated Texas Instruments Digital Signal Processing (DSP) board, TMS320C6713, instead of the usual microcontroller setup.

Recent technologies by Y. Pamungkas and Y. Rais (2022) implemented a real-time 
sound source localization system using the Interaural Time Difference Method, where two 
microphones spaced apart like human ears. To handle the heavy computation of GCC-PHAT 
without lagging, the researchers used a dedicated Texas Instruments Digital Signal Processing 
(DSP) board, TMS320C6713, instead of the usual microcontroller setup. The researchers wanted 
to prove that a minimal two-microphone setup could accurately localize sound in real-time.

Another technology by Villladangos et al. (2011) developed an indoor Local Positioning 
System (LPS) using ultrasonic beacons. To track the position of a mobile receiver, the system 
calculates the Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) of the acoustic signals emitted by different 
beacons. It then uses hyperbolic trilateration to pinpoint the receiver's exact spatial coordinates.

2.1.4 Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) 
Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) is defined as the difference in the arrival times of a 
propagating signal (such as an acoustic signal) measured across a specific pair of spatially 
separated sensors (such as microphones). In passive acoustic localization, this measured time 
difference is used to calculate the range difference between the sound source and the receiving 
nodes. This generates a set of hyperbolic equations, and the solution to these equations reveals 
the physical coordinates of the target (L. Dong et al. 2020).

One method of TDOA from (F. Yang and R. Song 2023) uses a Ternary Microphone 
Array Positioning Method, where three microphones are arranged in a straight line. Then, it uses 
the geometric relationship of the sound source  and the three microphones

turns.question: Fair enough; looking at your literature review regarding the RESAAW project by Rathna et al., which utilizes four DC vibrator motors for haptic feedback, I am concerned about the long-term wearability of such a system. How did you account for the potential for haptic sensory adaptation or physical irritation when designing your own feedback mechanism, given that users would be expected to wear this for daily, extended periods?
turns.grounding_reference: Rathna et al. (2024), which uses four omnidirectional microphones and an Arduino Uno board to detect sounds in the environment and provides directional haptic feedback using four DC vibrator motors

Other works have focused on bulkier head-worn devices that are specifically suited to 
particular outdoor/work scenarios. For example, in the study of Sun & Luo (2024), a smart helmet 
was developed using an embedded system to facilitate the safe journey of deaf pedestrians and 
cyclists by detecting sounds that could be potential hazards. However, as illustrated by the 
system's hardware footprint in Figure 2.14, integrating multiple modules into a helmet 
necessitates a bulky internal processing board. In a very specialized work environment, Elelu et 
al. (2024) have developed a multi-channel audio processing wearable device utilizing an ECU to 
identify and localize struck-by hazards, such as moving heavy equipment, to protect construction 
workers.

on embedded system. 2024 IEEE 4th International Conference on Electronic Technology, 
Communication and Information (ICETCI).)

Although these devices are quite effective in recording the surrounding environmental 
sounds, the physical form factor and feedback system have some drawbacks for day-to-day 
usage. For instance, head-mounted devices in the form of helmets are quite clunky and 
inconvenient for indoor usage. In addition to that, assistive smart glasses that make use of visual 
feedback in the form of LEDs have some drawbacks in that they always require the user's 
attention. This has the unintended side effect of increasing the cognitive load and distracting the 
user from the physical environment.

Keeping in view the downsides of visual dependency, recent research has also focused 
more on tactile and local alerting devices. In this regard, Rathna et al. (2024) have designed a 
Real-time Smart Auditory Assistive Wearable (RESAAW), which uses four omnidirectional 
microphones and an Arduino Uno board to detect sounds in the environment and provides 
directional haptic feedback using four DC vibrator motors, as shown in the prototype setup in
